newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel official warns on 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel official warns on 1997 budget.

text.p: A key Bank of Israel official warned on Thursday that the government's 1997 budget relied too much on higher taxes and not enough on spending cuts.

"A cautious monetary policy is required in ensure the government's multi-year inflationary targets," said Leo Lederman, head of the bank's research department, in a summary of his speech released by the bank.
His remarks, for delivery at a conference in Herzliya in the evening, come as the capital market awaits the central bank's response to the 1997 budget approved by parliament on January 1.
The Bank of Israel cut the short term base rate 0.5 percentage point to 14.7 percent days before the budget vote and will be announcing its February monetary programme on Janaury 27.

The government is committed to an inflationary target of 7-10 percent this year, which it hopes to achieve by seven billion shekels in budget cuts, higher taxes and other revenue measures included in the 1997 spending package.
But Lederman said the Bank of Israel estimated that more than half the seven billion shekels in savings came from higher taxes and other revenue-raising measures.
"In this context, initial estimates are that the tax burden will rise in 1997 by nearly one percent of gross domestic product at a time when the tax burden is already very high," said the summary.

"It must be stressed that the side effect of the structure of the chosen (budget) cut is an expected decline in the private savings rate as a percentage in disposable income....This comes at a time when, that for medium- and long-term considerations, it is important to encourage private savings," he said.
He said overall national savings would show a slight rise this year only because of an improvement in public sector saving.

Lederman urged the government to exercise strong controls over implementation of the budget and related issues such as privatisation and economic restructuring over the course of the year. These reviews, he said, should be conducted on a quarterly basis.
